X1.name: Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Boat Owners
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios.
X1.sample: 300 U.S. boat owners (owning a boat at least once) recruited via an online panel, balanced for region and ownership frequency.
X1.measure: Willingness to pay (WTP) for a consumer distress beacon at three price points ($50, $75, $100) and two messaging frames: (1) life-saving necessity; (2) cost-of-insurance savings.

prediction_by_theory.T1: WTP at $50 will be highest when framed as life-saving necessity, and WTP will increase with price up to $75 before declining at $100.
prediction_by_theory.T2: WTP at $50 will be highest when framed as cost-of-insurance savings, and WTP will increase with price up to $75 before declining at $100.

X1.decision_rule: If the average WTP at $50 for the life-saving frame exceeds $60 and is significantly higher than the WTP at $50 for the cost frame (difference >= $10), proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting life-saving use. If the cost frame's WTP at $50 is >= $65 and is significantly higher than the life frame's WTP at $50 (difference >= $10), proceed with a cost‑of‑insurance proposition. If neither condition is met, do not expand.

revisions.reason: Simulated warehouse test (SYN-D) concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer demand, insurance costs, or life-saving necessity. Therefore it provides no evidence for or against T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. arguments.name: Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Boat Owners
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios.
arguments.sample: 300 U.S. boat owners (owning a boat at least once) recruited via an online panel, balanced for region and ownership frequency.
arguments.measure: Willingness to pay (WTP) for a consumer distress beacon at three price points ($50, $75, $100) and two messaging frames: (1) life-saving necessity; (2) cost-of-insurance savings.

prediction_by_theory.T1: WTP at $50 will be highest when framed as life-saving necessity, and WTP will increase with price up to $75 before declining at $100.
prediction_by_theory.T2: WTP at $50 will be highest when framed as cost-of-insurance savings, and WTP will increase with price up to $75 before declining at $100.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average WTP at $50 for the life-saving frame exceeds $60 and is significantly higher than the WTP at $50 for the cost frame (difference >= $10), proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting life-saving use. If the cost frame's WTP at $50 is >= $65 and is significantly higher than the life frame's WTP at $50 (difference >= $10), proceed with a cost‑of‑insurance proposition. If neither condition is met, do not expand.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of existing consumer reach, market demand, competitive landscape, and technical feasibility.
Evidence must address whether a differentiated proposition would create measurable demand or value capture.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale landscaping, homeowner gardening).
2) Expand existing dealer network to reach more individual buyers without a differentiated proposition.
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current B2B/agricultural markets.
4) Partner with or license Deere technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than selling directly.
5) Target a different customer group (e.g., small‑farm owners) with a differentiated proposition.

T1.claim: Households adopt garden tractors because they are increasingly willing to pay for convenience and convenience, and Deere can capture value by selling directly through dealers and commanding premium prices.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners with small gardens who need easy, affordable landscaping.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing household income and changing lifestyles make garden work a worthwhile purchase; a differentiated proposition signals convenience and quality.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere sells tractors and attachments through dealers, earning margin on each unit and attachment sold.
assumptions: Households in 1962 have discretionary spending for gardening.
Deere can differentiate its tractors from competitors through design or service.
Dealers can reach individual buyers effectively.
predictions: If a differentiated proposition is offered, homeowner purchases of garden tractors will increase relative to baseline.
Deere's dealer margin per unit will be higher than for agricultural tractors.
Competitor sales will decline in the target segment.
T1.first_claim: Households adopt garden tractors because they are increasingly willing to pay for convenience and convenience, and Deere can capture value by selling directly through dealers and commanding premium prices.

T2.claim: Households adopt garden tractors because they need a reliable, durable tool for a specific chore (e.g., mowing, snow clearing), and Deere can capture value by selling through dealers and offering attachments that extend the tractor’s useful life.
T2.who_benefits: Homeowners with recurring gardening tasks who want a tool that lasts.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Growing household income and changing lifestyles make a single, reliable tool for a specific chore a worthwhile purchase; a differentiated proposition signals durability and versatility.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Deere sells tractors and attachments through dealers, earning margin on each unit and attachment sold, and can bundle services or spare parts.
assumptions: Homeowners in 1962 have recurring gardening needs that justify a dedicated tool.
Deere can differentiate its tractors through durability and attachment compatibility.
Dealers can provide after‑sale support for homeowner use.
predictions: If a differentiated proposition emphasizes durability and attachments, homeowner purchases will increase relative to a baseline without attachment focus.
Deere's attachment sales will be higher than for agricultural attachments.
Competitor sales will decline in the homeowner segment.

X1.name: Differentiated vs. Durability Proposition Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario.
X1.sample: 200 homeowners (100 per group) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, income, and gardening frequency.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and maximum price willingness to pay (WTP).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Differentiated proposition group will show higher purchase intent and WTP than durability proposition group.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Durability proposition group will show higher purchase intent and WTP than differentiated proposition group.

X1.decision_rule: If the differentiated proposition group achieves purchase intent >= 30% and WTP >= $1,500, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the durability proposition group achieves purchase intent >= 30% and WTP >= $1,500, develop a durability-focused proposition. If neither meets the thresholds, do not expand.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public sources show a 1962 lawn equipment sales surge (76%) and Deere's 1960 4010 tractor was the most popular, but they do not prove households are willing to pay a premium for a differentiated proposition. Conduct the proposed differentiated vs. durability proposition test before committing capital.
final.target_customer: Homeowners with small gardens who need easy, affordable landscaping.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated proposition that emphasizes convenience, quality, and dealer support, leveraging Deere's tractor engineering to offer a premium-priced, reliable garden tractor.
final.next_action: Run the 6‑week, €15,000 online survey test comparing differentiated vs. durability propositions, using purchase intent and willingness to pay as decision criteria.
final.uncertainty: Whether households in 1962 are willing to pay a premium for a differentiated proposition, and whether Deere can capture value through direct dealer sales.
would_change_if: If the test shows the durability proposition achieving purchase intent >= 30% and WTP >= $1,500, we would shift to a durability-focused proposition.
If the test shows neither proposition meeting the thresholds, we would maintain the status quo and not expand.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of existing consumer reach, market demand, competitive landscape, and technical feasibility.
Evidence must address whether a differentiated proposition would create measurable demand or value capture.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale landscaping, homeowner gardening).
2) Expand existing dealer network to reach more individual buyers without a differentiated proposition.
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current B2B/agricultural markets.
4) Partner with or license Deere technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than selling directly.
5) Target a different customer group (e.g., small‑farm owners) with a differentiated proposition.

They are willing to pay a premium for a brand they perceive as reliable.
The market size for small‑scale gardening is large enough to justify production.
predictions: If offered a differentiated lawn tractor, a measured percentage of households will express intent to purchase within a specified timeframe.

X1.name: Consumer Proposition Preference Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated product offering and choice-based conjoint analysis.
X1.sample: 500 households in the United States who have a small garden or garden space, recruited via an online panel.
X1.measure: 1) Intent to purchase a differentiated lawn tractor (binary: would buy). 2) Willingness to pay a premium (percentage willing to pay at $1,200 vs $800). 3) Number of units intended to purchase (binary: would buy one, two, or three).

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 30% will express intent to purchase a differentiated model, and willingness to pay premium will be at least 10% higher than for a standard model.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 30% will express intent to purchase multiple units (two or three), and willingness to pay premium will be at least 10% higher than for a standard model.

X1.decision_rule: If intent to purchase a differentiated model exceeds 30% and willingness to pay premium is at least 10% higher than for a standard model, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition. If intent is below 20% or premium willingness to pay is not significantly higher, do not invest.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. The evidence shows a growing market for lawn and garden equipment (76% sales rise, 1960‑99) and the 4010 model was the most popular, indicating demand. However, no source shows households are willing to pay a premium for a differentiated brand or that they view tractors as a status symbol. A low‑cost test is needed to measure intent and willingness.
final.target_customer: Households with small gardens who need easy, affordable gardening solutions.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated lawn tractor offering convenience, reliability, and brand trust, positioned as a practical solution for small‑scale gardening tasks.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Proposition Preference Test (500 households, $18,000, 10 weeks) to validate intent to purchase and willingness to pay premium.
final.uncertainty: The willingness of households to pay a premium for a differentiated brand and their motivation to purchase as a status symbol are unknown. The test will resolve these uncertainties.
would_change_if: If the test shows intent to purchase below 20% or willingness to pay premium is not significantly higher than for a standard model, the investment would be reconsidered.
If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for multiple‑unit purchases or premium pricing, the strategy would shift toward a differentiated proposition targeting multiple uses.

X1.name: Consumer Proposition Test: Status vs. Practicality
X1.method: Randomized controlled trial with two parallel offers to individual consumers in a small town. Each participant sees one offer describing a Deere lawn tractor positioned differently: (A) as a practical, low-cost gardening tool for small gardens; (B) as a status symbol for modern home ownership. Both offers include the same price point. Participants indicate whether they would purchase the offer and
X1.sample: 50 participants, recruited from a local community, balanced for age and gender. Each participant views one offer and provides a binary purchase decision.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and stated willingness to pay (WTP) in dollars for the differentiated feature. Secondary measure: self-reported reason for purchase (status vs. practicality).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Participants viewing the practical offer will have higher purchase intent and WTP than those viewing the status offer, indicating demand driven by cost and practicality.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Participants viewing the status offer will have higher purchase intent and WTP than those viewing the practical offer, indicating demand driven by status and lifestyle.

X1.decision_rule: If the difference in purchase intent between the two offers is statistically significant (p < 0.05) and the status offer achieves at least 15% higher intent than the practical offer, proceed with a differentiated status proposition. If the difference is not significant, do not invest in a differentiated proposition.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. A limited test is needed to confirm demand.

final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Proposition Test: Status vs. Practicality to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a differentiated offer.
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market and whether Deere can capture higher margins without cannibalizing B2B sales remain uncertain. Evidence of consumer preference for Deere over competitors is also lacking.
would_change_if: If the test shows a statistically significant difference in purchase intent between the practical and status offers, and the status offer achieves at least 15% higher intent, we would reconsider investing in a differentiated proposition.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. The evidence shows Deere already produced a lawn tractor in 1963 and entered the consumer market in the 1960s, but it does not demonstrate homeowner demand or willingness to pay a premium. A limited test (e.g., purchase intent survey) is needed to validate demand before committing resources.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of existing consumer reach, market demand, competitive landscape, and technical feasibility.
Evidence must address whether a differentiated proposition would create measurable demand or value capture.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale landscaping, homeowner gardening).
2) Expand existing dealer network to reach more individual buyers without a differentiated proposition.
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current B2B/agricultural markets.
4) Partner with or license Deere technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than selling directly.
5) Target a different customer group (e.g., small‑farm owners) with a differentiated proposition.

assumptions: Homeowners in 1962 have discretionary income to purchase a lawn tractor.
Deere can produce a consumer‑grade tractor that meets homeowner expectations for durability and ease of use.
Retail distribution exists to reach individual buyers.
predictions: If a test offers a consumer‑grade lawn tractor, at least 20% of surveyed homeowners will express intent to purchase.
Sales of the consumer model will be higher than sales of a comparable non‑differentiated tractor in the same period.

X1.name: Consumer vs Farmowner Purchase Intent Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to a consumer‑grade lawn tractor (T1) and a small‑farm owner‑grade lawn tractor (T2). Participants are recruited from a panel of homeowners and small‑farm owners in the Midwest. Each participant sees one ad and is asked to indicate intent to purchase (1‑10 scale).
X1.sample: 200 participants: 100 homeowners (mid‑10‑age, moderate income) and 100 small‑farm owners (small farms, limited budget).
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and willingness to pay (EUR).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Homeowners will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than small‑farm owners for the consumer model.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Small‑farm owners will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than homeowners for the farm‑owner model.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent for the consumer model among homeowners is at least 10 points higher than for the farm‑owner model, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 5 points, treat both models as equal and do not invest in a differentiated offer. If the difference is less than 3 points, consider no expansion and focus on existing B2B/agricultural markets.

final.uncertainty: The size of the homeowner market and their willingness to pay a premium for a differentiated model are unknown. Small‑farm owner demand is also uncertain due to limited data on their purchase behavior.
